candidate_relations.reason: Miller Fisher syndrome is a GBS variant defined by ophthalmoplegia/ataxia/areflexia, incompatible with this pure motor axonal picture.
Acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy is the demyelinating GBS subtype, not acute motor axonal neuropathy.
Acute motor axonal neuropathy is identical to the reference diagnosis.
Motor axonopathy is a parent description missing the acute GBS-spectrum AMAN identity.
Guillain-Barré syndrome is the parent syndrome but omits the required motor-axonal subtype.
Acute stroke was a reasonable initial concern given hypertension but imaging was repeatedly normal.
Acute flaccid paralysis describes the motor phenotype without identifying AMAN.
Spinal cord injury is not supported by normal cervical imaging and areflexic spreading limb weakness.
Poliomyelitis is a related acute flaccid paralysis with incompatible infectious anterior-horn identity.
Pharyngeal-cervical-brachial syndrome is a different GBS regional variant; cranial-bulbar features were absent at onset.
Botulism was considered and serum toxin testing was negative, and the course was areflexic limb paralysis.
Transverse myelitis is a myelopathy, not a peripheral motor axonopathy, and spine imaging was unremarkable.
Acute motor axonal polyneuropathy is a synonymous label for acute motor axonal neuropathy.
Stroke remains excluded by serial brain MRI including diffusion imaging.
Myasthenia gravis does not produce rapidly spreading areflexic flaccid paralysis after a post-infectious prodrome.
Spinal cord infarction is inconsistent with normal cord imaging and subsequent generalized areflexia.
Classical GBS (AIDP) names the demyelinating subtype, incompatible with AMAN.
Acute motor-sensory axonal neuropathy requires sensory involvement; sensation remained intact.
Acute flaccid myelitis is a myelopathic process, not AMAN, and cord imaging was normal.
Acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy is the demyelinating GBS form, not AMAN.
